title: Module 13 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: A statistically significant correlation must be strong.
items.why: With a large sample, a very small r can be significant. Report r and r squared too.

items.s: A reliable measure is automatically a valid measure.
items.why: A scale can give consistent scores and still measure the wrong thing.

items.s: A measure cannot be valid unless it is reasonably reliable.
items.why: Inconsistent scores cannot reflect a stable construct.

items.s: The same r can be significant with n = 100 but not significant with n = 15.
items.why: The critical value of r decreases as n increases.

items.s: Spearman's correlation is a better choice than Pearson's when the data are ordinal.
items.why: It uses the ranks and does not assume interval scale data.

items.s: A significant correlation means the null hypothesis that rho = 0 is proven false.
items.why: It means the data are unlikely if rho = 0. It is not proof.

items.s: Test-retest reliability is shown by correlating scores from the same people at two times.
items.why: A high correlation indicates stable scores.

items.s: Whether a significant but small correlation of .10 is meaningful
items.why: It depends on context, since small effects can matter for large populations. It accounts for only 1 percent of the variance, so it predicts individuals poorly.
